canonical_topic: Call and put payoff mechanics relative to the strike price
definition: Every option has a strike (exercise) price — the fixed price at which the underlying can be traded in the future. A call option pays off when the market price rises above the strike, letting the owner buy cheap and resell at the higher market price. A put option pays off when the market price falls below the strike, letting the owner sell high relative to the market; if the market price is above the strike, the put is worthless since no one would sell for less than market value.
core_idea: Call value increases as the underlying rises above the strike; put value increases as the underlying falls below the strike — each option only has value when exercising it beats the prevailing market price.
key_points: Strike/exercise price = the fixed future trading price set in the contract.
Call owner benefits when market price > strike, buying low (at strike) and able to resell at the higher market price.
Put owner benefits when market price < strike, selling high (at strike) rather than at the lower market price.
A put is worthless if the market price is above the strike, since no one would voluntarily sell below market value.
relationships: Builds directly on the call/put definition item
trading_implications: Whether an option is worth exercising is a straightforward comparison of strike versus current market price, per the author — the hard problem is pricing the option beforehand, not deciding when to exercise it.
